deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a draft in Riemann's natural-philosophical (metaphysical) notes, under the heading 'Allgemeine Sätze über das Wirken' (general propositions about acting or causal efficacy). It continues a numbered list of theses whose item I is on an earlier sheet; item II is struck out. The previous sheet carries a Lucretius motto (De rerum natura I.52-53), and the next sheet concludes the discussion.

Structure of the argument:
(III) The theses concern the case where the agent (Agens) is a being, something capable of change.
(IV) Such an action, which produces a state or a change, can obviously take place only on things capable of an equal or like state.
(V) On which of these things it acts, and whether it acts at all, cannot be inferred from the concept of the agent alone.

Section 'zur Erklärung der Veränderungen' (for explaining changes). These propositions hold only if an agent foreign to the thing must be assumed. If two things a and b are brought by an external ground into an immediate connection in which they did not stand before, a consequence c can be attached to it. This c is determined neither by the concept of a alone nor by that of b alone. Struck variants say c ceases when the connection ceases, or persists as long as the connections are unchanged. In modern terms (my gloss): c is an emergent, relational effect, a function of the pair (a,b) and their connection, not decomposable into separate contributions of a and b.

Section 'Einfachste Art des Wirkens' (simplest kind of acting). These propositions hold only if the acting is ascribed to a simple real ground (Realgrund, Herbart's term). If a and b enter into connection through a single ground, the consequence c can be attached to one of the following:
- the connection, i.e. the being-connected (Verbundensein), itself; or
- the change of its degree (Grad).
The struck alternatives also list the act of connecting (Verbinden). The page ends with the 'simplest assumption': c is attached to the being-connected, and presumably ceases when it ceases (the wording here is fragmentary and partly struck).

The next page states the guiding principle: what an agent strives to bring about must be determined by its concept. Riemann applies it not, as Leibniz and Spinoza did, to beings with manifold determinations, but to real grounds of the greatest possible simplicity. This is a Herbartian framework of simple 'Realen', their 'Zusammen' (being together) and the resulting effects.

In physical terms (my interpretation, not explicit on the page), the distinction is between two options:
- an effect depending on the state of connection, as with a potential depending on configuration;
- an effect depending on the rate of change of the degree of connection, as with velocity-dependent action.
This matches Riemann's known interest in action laws of Weber type.
errors: No mathematical steps to check. Logically, the argument is coherent but heavily revised. Item II is wholly struck, and several alternative formulations of when c ceases are crossed out without a clear final version. The last sentence is incomplete.

results.what: Thesis that an effect c of the connection of two things a, b is determined neither by the concept of a nor of b alone: a relational, non-decomposable effect.
results.modern_name: relational or emergent causation (Herbartian 'Zusammen der Realen')
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart (Allgemeine Metaphysik, 1828-29); background in Leibniz

results.what: Classification of what an effect of connection may attach to (the being-connected itself, or the change of its degree), choosing the being-connected as the simplest assumption.
results.modern_name: state-dependent vs. rate-dependent interaction (loosely: potential vs. velocity-dependent forces)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's philosophical fragments (published in part in Gesammelte Werke, 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts', 1876)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of Riemann's Herbart-influenced natural philosophy, whose themes (Realgrund, simplest acting, critique of Leibniz/Spinoza) are known from the published philosophical fragments. There is no mathematical content. It is at most a minor unpublished variant formulation.

checkable.asserts: Illustrative modern gloss only, not on the page: an effect c(a,b)=a*b is not of the form f(a)+g(b). This is one way to formalize 'determined neither by a nor by b alone'.

transcription_corrections: Heading 'Allgemeine Sätze über das Wirken' is written above the struck line II and governs the list.
Line III likely reads 'wenn das Agens ein Wesen (ein Veränderliches) ist', with a small interlinear insertion. The reading '{+ihm+}' is uncertain.

Line IV is better read: 'Eine solche Aktion (einen Zustand oder eine Veränderung, deren Wechsel ... bewirkt) kann selbstredend nur auf solche Dinge stattfinden, die eines gleichen Zustandes fähig sind'.
The '(c)' after 'Folge' is circled in the manuscript. The folio number 92 is circled at the right margin.
In the second section the fragment '...derung ihres Grades' is the continuation of 'Verän-' (Veränderung ihres Grades) across the line break; 'das Ge' is struck.
The final sentence reads roughly 'Die einfachste Annahme ist, daß die Folge c an das Verbundensein geknüpft [sei] ...', the rest struck or incomplete.
